title: Compound Personal Pronouns
subtitle: Eight words ending in -self, and the job they do for emphasis.
objectives: List the eight compound personal pronouns
Use a compound personal pronoun for emphasis
Explain why hisself and theirselves are not words
Avoid using myself in place of me
Retell Don Quixote Chapter 6 and explain what Sancho is promised

cards.title: Add -self to a pronoun and it gets a new job
cards.text: Me becomes myself. They become themselves. Eight words, built the same way, and they do two different jobs.

cards.title: Take the pronoun and add -self or -selves
cards.text: Singular ones end in -self. Plural ones end in -selves. There are no exceptions to that part.
points: **Singular:** myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself.
**Plural:** ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
**Eight in total.** Learn them as a set.
***Yourself* and *yourselves*** are different words.

cards.title: Cross it out and see what survives
cards.text: Three tabs. The last one is the full list. Two quiz questions come from this.

question.text: Which of these is NOT a real word?
question.explain: Hisself and theirselves are not words. The correct forms are himself and themselves.

cards.title: Emphasis: the intensive use
cards.text: Here the word adds force and nothing else. It sits next to the noun it is emphasising, or at the end.
points: **"The principal *herself* handed out the prizes."**
**"I built it *myself*."**
**Remove it and the sentence still works.**
**That removal test** is how you spot the intensive use.

cards.title: "He wrapped his own hands" versus "he wrapped them himself"
cards.text: Both are correct and they mean slightly different things. The second one is answering somebody who assumed otherwise.
points: **Emphasis usually answers an unspoken question.**
**"The coach *himself* came down"** — not an assistant.
**Nobody says it** unless the contrast matters.
**That is what the word is for.**

question.text: In "The captain himself apologised", what is himself doing?
options: Adding emphasis — it could be removed
Acting as the object of the verb
question.explain: Remove it and "the captain apologised" still works. That is the intensive use.

cards.title: Myself is not a polite word for me
cards.text: "Please contact myself" is wrong, and it is everywhere in emails. Myself only works if you are also the subject.
points: **Wrong:** "Send it to myself."
**Right:** "Send it to me."
**Right:** "I sent it to myself." *I* am the subject.
**It is not more formal.** It is just wrong.

options: Please give the form to me
Please give the form to myself
Please give the form to I
Please give the form to mine
question.explain: Myself needs I to be the subject of the same sentence. Here there is no I at all.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Grammar done. Part 2 is Chapter 6, where he finally finds somebody to come with him. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Chapter 6: The Choosing of a Squire
cards.text: Home again and recovering, he works out what was missing from the first two trips. Every knight in the books had a squire.

cards.title: Sancho Panza
cards.text: A neighbour. A poor farm labourer with a wife and children, no education, and no interest at all in chivalry.
points: **He is not a knight** and never pretends to be.
**He rides a donkey**, not a horse.
**He is practical where Don Quixote is not.**
**That contrast is the engine of the whole book.**

cards.title: An island to govern
cards.text: Don Quixote promises that when he conquers an island, Sancho will be made its governor. Sancho believes him.
points: **Knights in the books did hand out islands.**
**So the promise is consistent** with his world.
**Sancho leaves without telling his wife properly.**
**They set off at night**, so nobody sees.

question.text: What does Don Quixote promise Sancho Panza?
options: A place at the king's court
question.explain: The governorship of an island. It is exactly the kind of reward knights hand out in the books he reads.

cards.title: The book only really starts here
cards.text: For five chapters he has been alone, which means nobody can disagree with him out loud. Sancho changes that on page one.
points: **One character cannot argue** with himself convincingly.
**Sancho sees windmills.** Don Quixote sees giants.
**Now there are two versions** of every event.
**Give your character somebody to be wrong at.**

cards.title: He is the second player, not a follower
cards.text: A companion who agrees with everything adds nothing. Sancho is useful because he is running a completely different plan.
points: **He is in it for the island.** That is all.
**He never believes in the giants.**
**He comes anyway**, which is the interesting part.
**Two goals in one party** makes the story move.

question.text: Sancho Panza believes in knights and chivalry as strongly as Don Quixote does.
question.explain: False. He is a practical farm labourer who has come along for the promised island.

terms.def: A pronoun ending in -self or -selves. There are eight.
The -self word adds emphasis only. Remove it and the sentence survives.
The -self word is the object of the verb. Next week's topic.
Not words. The correct forms are himself and themselves.
A knight's attendant. Sancho Panza is Don Quixote's.
The island Don Quixote promises Sancho he will govern.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Eight words:** -self singular, -selves plural.
**Intensive means removable.** Cross it out and check.
**Hisself and theirselves do not exist.**
**Sancho comes for the island**, not the chivalry.

quiz.text: How many compound personal pronouns are there?
quiz.explain: Five singular and three plural: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
quiz.objective: List the eight compound personal pronouns

quiz.text: Which is the correct plural form for more than one person you are speaking to?
quiz.explain: Yourself is singular, yourselves is plural. English keeps both, and the exam checks it.

quiz.text: Which of these is NOT a word?
quiz.explain: Theirselves and hisself are not words. Use themselves and himself.
quiz.objective: Explain why hisself and theirselves are not words

quiz.explain: Himself. There is no such word as hisself, however often it is said.
quiz.objective: Explain why hisself and theirselves are not words

quiz.text: In "The author herself replied", what is herself doing?
options: Adding emphasis, and it could be removed
Acting as the object of the verb
quiz.explain: Remove it and the sentence still works. That is the intensive use.
quiz.objective: Use a compound personal pronoun for emphasis

quiz.text: An intensive pronoun can be removed without breaking the sentence.
quiz.explain: True, and that removal test is the most reliable way to identify one.
quiz.objective: Use a compound personal pronoun for emphasis

options: Please send the report to me
Please send the report to myself
Please send the report to I
Please send the report to mine
quiz.explain: Myself needs I as the subject of the same sentence. Here there is none, so it must be me.
quiz.objective: Avoid using myself in place of me

options: Contact myself if you need help
Ana and myself went to the shop
quiz.explain: I is the subject and myself is the object. That is the only case where it works.
quiz.objective: Avoid using myself in place of me

quiz.explain: Sancho Panza, a poor neighbour with a wife, children and no interest in chivalry.
quiz.objective: Retell Don Quixote Chapter 6 and explain what Sancho is promised

quiz.text: What is Sancho promised in return for coming?
quiz.explain: The governorship of an island. Knights in the books he reads hand out exactly that.
quiz.objective: Retell Don Quixote Chapter 6 and explain what Sancho is promised

quiz.text: Sancho Panza believes he is riding out to become a knight.
quiz.explain: False. He is a farm labourer, he rides a donkey, and he has come for the island.
quiz.objective: Retell Don Quixote Chapter 6 and explain what Sancho is promised

quiz.text: Why does Sancho's arrival change the book?
options: There are now two versions of every event
He can read the books too
quiz.explain: Alone, nobody could contradict Don Quixote out loud. Sancho sees windmills where he sees giants.
quiz.objective: Retell Don Quixote Chapter 6 and explain what Sancho is promised

teacher.summary: Week 6 English covers compound personal pronouns alongside Don Quixote Chapter 6, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. The lesson deliberately takes only the intensive use, leaving the reflexive use to Week 7, so the two weeks are genuinely different rather than a repeat. The selfPronouns figure carries the deletion test, which is the only reliable way to tell the two uses apart and is far more useful than a definition. The 'myself' error is included because it is endemic in adult writing and email, and naming it now is the cheapest time to fix it. NOTE ON THE TEXT: the school's edition is abridged and its chapter numbering does not match Cervantes' original, so this lesson follows the episode named in the title rather than any original chapter number.
discussion: Ask him to cross out the -self word in a few sentences and say whether they survive. The test is the lesson.
Ask why 'contact myself' sounds formal but is wrong. Sounding formal and being correct are unrelated.
Ask what Sancho actually wants. He is not there for chivalry, and noticing that changes how the rest reads.
Ask why a story needs two characters who disagree. It is the most useful writing lesson in the book.
teacher.extension: Have him write four sentences using intensive pronouns where the emphasis genuinely answers an unspoken objection. Emphasis without a contrast sounds odd, and finding that out is the exercise.
misconceptions: 'Hisself and theirselves are informal versions.' They are not words at all.
'Myself is a polite way of saying me.' It only works when I am also the subject of the sentence.
'Yourself covers both singular and plural.' Yourselves exists and the exam checks it.
'Sancho believes in knights.' He is practical and sceptical. He came for the promised island.
